transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Before we get started, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what’s brought me in is… I keep finding myself getting up when I really should just stay seated. Like in staff meetings at school, everyone’s sitting there and I suddenly think I need to refill my coffee or check a handout at the back of the room. And at dinner too, I’ll pop up for something that isn’t really urgent.

It sounds small when I say it out loud, but it keeps happening, and I’m starting to feel a bit embarrassed by it.
When you feel the need to get up, do you notice an uncomfortable or crawling sensation in your legs that gets better once you move, or is it more just a mental urge to be doing something?

No, I wouldn’t say it’s a crawling feeling in my legs or anything like that. It’s more… I suddenly feel I ought to be doing something. Like in a meeting I’ll think, “Oh, I should refill my coffee,” or “I’ll just check that handout at the back,” even though it’s not really important right then.

Same at dinner, I’ll get up for something small, and then I realize everyone else is still sitting. It’s more in my head than in my legs, if that makes sense.

When you feel that urge to get up and do something, do you also notice yourself worrying or feeling anxious about something at that moment, or does the urge come on without any particular worried thoughts?

It doesn’t usually feel like worry, no. I mean, I might be thinking about a dozen little things, but not anxious exactly. It’s more that I suddenly decide I should do something — refill my coffee, check something at the back of the room, grab a handout — and then I’m up before I’ve really thought it through.

At dinner it’s similar. I’ll just pop up for some small thing, and then notice everyone else is still sitting there. It’s not really because something urgent is wrong. It’s just this push to be moving or doing something.

Aside from these urges to get up and move, do you also notice trouble staying focused on tasks—like losing your train of thought during meetings, being easily distracted, or frequently forgetting what you were doing?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, exactly. I mean, meetings can be a bit dull sometimes—especially the ones about timetabling, those seem to go in circles forever—but I haven’t really noticed losing my train of thought as the main problem.

It’s more the getting up bit that stands out to me. Though now that you ask, I suppose everyone gets distracted sometimes, don’t they? Especially in a school, there’s always someone knocking on the door or a bell going off. But I can’t say I’ve been keeping track of that, really.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others mid-conversation, blurting out responses before someone finishes speaking, or having trouble waiting your turn in line or discussions?

Yes, I do that, I’m afraid. Mostly in group discussions — like my book club, or curriculum meetings at school. Someone will be halfway through making a point and the answer is already right there in my head, and I just… jump in.

It’s not that I mean to be rude. Sometimes I only realise after, when they stop talking or look a bit surprised. Book club is especially bad because everyone has opinions, and then I’ve got my own thought about the ending or the author’s style — oh, we read one recently that everyone loved and I couldn’t see the fuss — but yes, I do blurt things out before people have quite finished.
Thinking back, do you remember having similar restlessness, impulsivity, or trouble waiting your turn when you were a child or teenager, even before you became a teacher?

Oh yes, I think so. I mean, it’s funny what you remember and what you don’t — I can still picture the classroom with those wooden desks, and the pencil sharpener on the wall, the sort with the little handle. My mother used to joke that I’d worn a path between my desk and that sharpener before I was ten.

And my report cards were always along the lines of, “bright girl, but needs to stay in her seat,” or “must wait her turn.” That sort of thing. At the time I think people just called it being lively, or chatty, especially for a girl. But yes, looking back, it was there when I was young.

Would you say these patterns—jumping up, interrupting, blurting things out—have actually caused real problems for you, like trouble at work, tension with colleagues or friends, or difficulties in your relationships?

Yes… I think it has, more than I’d like to admit. Not in a dramatic, losing-my-job sort of way, but it does affect things.

At work, in meetings, I can feel people getting a bit tired of me jumping in. Sometimes a colleague will give me that look — you know, the polite teacher look, we all have one — and I realise I’ve cut across them again. And then I leave feeling embarrassed, like I’ve made myself seem overbearing when I didn’t mean to.

It’s similar at book club. I go because I want to feel part of something, really, but if I blurt out too much or get ahead of everyone, people lose patience. Then I come home feeling less connected than when I went, which is a bit sad. So yes, it has caused some tension in work and in the community, I suppose.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports pervasive, longstanding hyperactive-impulsive symptoms—unwarranted urges to get up during meetings/meals, chronic interrupting and blurting out answers before others finish—that began in childhood ('needs to stay in her seat,' 'must wait her turn') and have persisted into adulthood, causing social and occupational friction (colleagues' annoyance, tension at book club). Restless movement lacks the sensory/dysesthetic quality typical of restless legs syndrome, and the urge to move is not accompanied by anxious cognitions, arguing against an anxiety-driven etiology. Inattentive symptoms (losing train of thought, forgetfulness) were not endorsed, so the presentation is best characterized as ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation (ICD-10 F90.0), with childhood onset and current functional impairment confirmed.
